title: Routing + Quantization Sweep: Long-context Insights across Llama/Mistral/Qwen
body:
Purpose and framing:
This doc collects early profiling results and observations from a coordinated sweep: how routing (MoE-style models and routing heuristics) interacts with quantized execution and long-context workloads on three representative architectures (Llama-2 family style, Mistral-like dense transformers, and Qwen-style models). Goal: surface cross-model patterns, explainable bottlenecks, and actionable mitigations we can prototype in the next 2 sprints.

Quick TL;DR:
- Observed recurring bottleneck: routing decision overhead + cache thrash dominates tail latency when sequence lengths exceed ~8k tokens and quantized kernels are used.
- Llama-style models (dense) are mostly compute-bound in attention + MLP steps; quantization helps but amplifies KV cache memory/locality effects.
- Mistral-like models show relatively better long-context scaling (smaller per-token latency growth) but become network/packing sensitive in multi-GPU setups.
- Qwen-style variants with deeper contexts and cross-layer attention variants reveal gating hot-spots in MoE routing that cause CPU stalls during expert index bookkeeping.
- Practical mitigations: lighter routing policies during long-context sessions, adaptive cache eviction knobs, micro-batching with sequence-aware scheduling, and selective dequantize paths for small control-plane ops.

Environment and benchmark setup:
- Hardware: G6A (A100S-equivalent) single-GPU for baseline; multi-GPU runs on DGX-style 8xA100 (NVLink). Also a small testbed on M40-class for stress/degenerate behavior.
- Runtime: internal serve v0.24.3 (local kernel selector), python runner wrapped with our tracing harness.
- Models: Llama-2-ish 13B dense (float32 + int8 sweep), Mistral-7B-like dense (fp16 baseline + int8), Qwen-14B-ish with MoE-style gating layer simulation (note: we used a synthetic MoE wrapper with 64 experts to emulate index patterns).
- Inputs: mixture of synthetic long prompts (2k, 4k, 8k, 16k tokens) and real-doc streams (customer anonymized logs).
- Metrics captured: p50/p90/p99 single-request latency, per-token latency breakdown (attention / MLP / KV cache ops / routing), CPU sys/user, GPU kernel occupancy, PCIe/NVLink transfer MB/s, memory pressure (GPU resident, host pinned).

Notable profiling traces and patterns:
1) Routing decision overhead (MoE wrapper)
- Pattern: when sequence length grows, per-token routing bookkeeping (gathering expert indices, updating per-expert counts, building scatter/gather indices) moved from ~2-3ms down to 10-15ms (p90) for long sequences.
- Cause: Python/CPU-side data-structure updates + repeated small memcpy to GPU with many micro-batches.
- Symptom: GPU sits waiting for index tensors; kernels are underutilized (occupancy drops to 30–40%).
- Quick check: replacing the Python routing handler with a fused CUDA kernel to compute routing indices lowered routing overhead by ~60% in the synthetic wrapper.

2) KV-cache locality and quantization interplay
- Observation: int8 quantized MLP/attention kernels reduce compute time but increase sensitivity to KV cache layout.
- Explanation hypothesis: quantized paths prefer packing and smaller working sets; however KV-cache read/write patterns for long contexts cause non-coalesced memory access, increasing effective memory latency. Result: token-level time for KV ops increases despite faster compute kernels.
- Evidence: memory bandwidth utilization spiked and more unaligned loads observed in GPU traces during long-context runs on quantized builds.

3) Llama-like dense models: compute vs memory balance
- Short contexts (<=2k): latency dominated by attention kernel time; quantization yields good token-level speedups (~20–35% improvement p50).
- Long contexts (>8k): attention query/key buildup causes O(n) memory operations that overshadow quant gains; KV eviction and pointer chasing on host-side increases jitter.
- Mitigation tested: prefix-compressed caching reduced memory working set and gave ~15% p90 improvement for 8k sequences.

4) Mistral-like models: packing, multi-GPU and network sensitivity
- Mistral-style smaller attention heads and more compact MLPs resulted in lower per-token compute. However, multi-GPU placement (sharded activations) amplified cross-GPU transfer.
- For long contexts, NVLink transfer and all-gather steps became visible contributors (~10–25% of p99).
- Recommended action: prefer model sharding schemes that minimize per-token cross-host traffic for long-pinned sessions; test pipeline parallel micro-batching to amortize all-gather.

5) Qwen-like (MoE gating) specific fail modes
- Synthetic MoE wrapper revealed hot expert churn: when expert selection distribution was skewed over a small subset, those experts blew up memory (per-expert buffers) and queueing latency spiked.
- Observed CPU-side enqueue/dequeue stalls because the routing metadata management was not batched; we hit syscalls per-request due to locking around expert queues.
- Workaround: introduce token-level pre-bucketing to reduce enqueue frequency; also experimented with lock-free ring buffers in C++ which reduced tail latency by ~30% p99.

6) Small-control ops and dequantize overhead
- Control-plane operations (routing bookkeeping, sequence-termination checks) frequently required dequantizing small tensors (int8->fp16) for compatibility with legacy kernels. These micro-dequant operations had disproportionate overhead.
- Suggestion: keep an "int8 control path" that executes bookkeeping in int32/int16 domain or uses pre-compiled lightweight kernels to avoid frequent dequantize/quantize thrash.

Experiment logs (short)
- 2025-01-14: Baseline dense (Llama-like 13B) fp16 vs int8 at 4k and 8k. Observed 28% mean speedup for int8 at 4k; at 8k the speedup reduced to 9%, p99 became worse by 12%.
- 2025-01-16: Swapped Python routing handler for fused CUDA prototype (MoE index gen). p90 routing overhead dropped from ~12ms->4.5ms.
- 2025-01-18: Introduced prefix-compression LRU for KV cache; for 8k sequences p90 improved ~15% for dense models, p99 unchanged.
- 2025-01-20: Multi-GPU Mistral-like run with pipeline micro-batching (batch size 4 microbatches). NVLink overhead amortized, p99 improved 18% for 16k sequences.

Open questions and unknowns:
- How does quantization-aware kernel layout impact KV caches fundamentally? The traces show more uncoalesced reads but we need lower-level memory access profiling (cupti-level) for confirmation.
- Is there an adaptive routing policy that can trade quality for less bookkeeping mid-session? Where do we draw the line (customer-configurable)?
- For real MoE (not synthetic wrapper), how do expert memory footprints vary across implementations (some frameworks pre-allocate per-expert buffers differently)? We need to replicate with a real MoE checkpoint.
- Cost/benefit of shipping an optimized fused routing kernel vs keeping routing in C++ but batched: which is easier to maintain?

Action items / next experiments:
- (Diego) instrument cupti memory-access patterns for quantized vs fp16 runs on 8k sequences (due 2025-01-28).
- (Sana) prototype int8 control-path kernels for routing bookkeeping (investigate overhead reduction; due 2025-02-04).
- (Ethan) run a real MoE checkpoint test with our fused routing kernel on 4xA100 to measure expert churn effects (due 2025-01-30).
- (Maya) add an end-to-end micro-batching schedule that is aware of current sequence length distribution and measures tradeoffs across p50/p99 (due 2025-02-07).

Notes-to-self / loose thoughts:
- Could we detect "long-context mode" early (e.g., token count > X) and switch to a light-weight routing policy or enable prefix-compression heuristics automatically? Need to measure false-positive risk for short-but-bursty flows.
- Consider exposing a runtime flag for "favor_tail_latency" vs "favor_mean_cost" which toggles kv eviction aggressiveness and routing batching thresholds. Useful for Dedicated customers with strict SLOs.
- Add an internal benchmark type: longstream (sequence length distribution heavy tail) to our benchmark suite.

References / links in-flight:
- Confluence: internal long-context design doc (CONFLUENCE-1254)
- GitHub PR: fused routing kernel prototype (https://github.com/redwood-inference/serve/pull/1934)
- JIRA: routing+quantization investigation epic (JIRA-RT-872)

Appendix: quick checklist for deploying mitigations in a canary
- Canary 1: enable fused routing kernel on a subset of hosts; monitor p99 routing and GPU occupancy.
- Canary 2: enable prefix-compression cache policy for long sessions only; measure token-throughput and OOM rates.
- Canary 3: route MoE-heavy requests to dedicated hosts with larger host memory and optimized lock-free queue implementation.

If you read nothing else: the interaction between routing bookkeeping (CPU-side) and quantized kernels (GPU-side) amplifies tail latency for long-context workloads. Fixing the routing path (fusing or porting to GPU/C++) and improving cache locality are the two highest-leverage items we can act on in the short term.

End of notes (working doc). This is intentionally sketchy; comments and pointers welcome.
